title: Ang 984–988: Mali Gaura
hookLine: a short raga with Namdev's hymns
tomorrow: a raga of courage opens. so why not with a war cry?

cards: Grandparents bless the strangest things: a new car, a backpack on the first day of school, a pot of dal before anyone eats.
Namdev does the same on ang 988, in Mali Gaura, a short raga near the end of this stretch of the Granth. In paraphrase: blessed is the flute the Lord plays, sweet, sweet, the unstruck sound.
And then: blessed is the wool, blessed the blanket Krishna wears.

teach.b: Mali Gaura opens on ang 984 with hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and then comes Namdev.
His hymn is a string of blessings, in paraphrase: blessed the flute; blessed the sheep's wool; blessed the blanket; blessed the mother Devaki, in whose home the Lord was born.
Ordinary things, made blessed because the Lord came near them.

teach.h: WHAT MAKES A SMALL THING HOLY?
teach.b: So, today's question: what makes a small thing holy? Namdev's answer is nearness. Wool is just wool until it wraps the Beloved.

Namdev's pictures come from a story Hindus tell in their own scripture, the Bhagavata Purana: Krishna, the young cowherd, playing his flute in the forest at night, and the cowherd women leaving everything behind to follow the sound.

In that telling too, the music is the divine call, and cows, milk pots and blankets are where the Lord is found. That's a real, shared instinct: holiness can live in the everyday, and a sound can be a call.
And an honest difference. For Krishna's devotees, Krishna himself is the Lord, loved in that form.
In the Granth, Namdev's hymn sits among hymns to the One who is never born, and Sikh readers hear the flute as that One's call.
Same flute in the picture. Different answers about who's playing.

how: Ragis sing Mali Gaura's hymns in kirtan; Namdev's hymn of the flute and the blessed blanket is sung as praise of the One, in Krishna's imagery.

blessed the flute, blessed the wool, blessed the blanket Krishna wears.
Sikhs and Hindus read the flute in exactly the same way
the picture is shared; Sikh readers hear the One beyond birth, Krishna's devotees love Krishna himself as the Lord.
holiness, for Namdev, is only found in temples
wool and a blanket are blessed because the Lord came near them.

games.q: at a friend's house you hear a song about Krishna's flute, and she asks if Sikhs have anything like it. what's your best answer?
o: yes: Namdev's hymn in the Granth blesses the flute too; Sikhs hear it as the One's call.
no; Krishna has nothing at all to do with the Guru Granth Sahib.
yes, it's the same song, so Sikhs and Hindus believe the same thing.
games.why: the flute is a real shared picture. the honest difference is who's playing: Krishna himself, for his devotees; the One beyond birth, for Sikh readers.

practice: If there's something sweet within reach, a raisin, a bit of fruit, a sip of tea, take one small taste and let it rest on your tongue for a few breaths before you swallow. Small and sweet, and fully noticed.
If you'd like, read ang 984 first, where the raga opens.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ben, flute; 'dhan dhan o raam ben baajai', blessed is that flute the Lord plays (ang 988).

carryVoice: Short and sweet: a small thing turns holy when the Beloved comes near it. Take it with you.
